en: Preface to the Brief Record of the Five Patriarchs of the Dharmadhātu School.
In the summer of the Gengshen year, while I was at the Seven Buddhas Hall, I was perusing the Tripitaka and reading the monastic histories.

One day, I inquired of Dharma Master Baiting of Ciyun regarding the five patriarchs of the Avataṃsaka school. Upon hearing his explanation, I harbored some doubts and therefore requested further instruction.

Before even ten days had passed since the compilation of the *Life of the Five Patriarchs*, the Dharma Master compiled a single volume titled *Brief Record*. Upon examining it, it became clear that the monastic histories (*sengshi*) were indeed inconsistent and erroneous.

For instance, regarding the Third Patriarch, the Great Master Xianshou, the tradition states that in the Bingshen year of the Dengfeng era, an imperial edict summoned the Master to lecture on the *New Sūtra* (the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*).

It further records that he was moved by a radiance from the Master’s mouth and an earthquake, and that the Emperor issued an edict for the Ten Virtuous Ones to confer the precepts upon him. Now, let us examine this according to the present record.
The new scripture was only translated during the Yiwu year of the Zhengsheng era; it was completed only at the beginning of the Jihai year of the Shenglì era.

How could it have been lectured upon before it had even been translated? Moreover, the Third Patriarch received the tonsure in the Gengwu year of the Xiánhéng era and began lecturing immediately upon receiving the imperial decree.
By the Bingshén year of the Dēngfēng era—twenty-seven years later—the Patriarch was fifty-four years old, and his Way had already filled the world, only then [did he...]
To claim that he received the precepts is unlikely to be true. Furthermore, the *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation for Returning to the Source) has been falsely attributed to the Venerable Dushun.
If the National Preceptor’s lifespan truly ended at seventy, as some claim, then the errors in the historical records are all too evident.
Later, I further investigated the original sources of the *Jueji* (Abridged Record). It states: "The first and second patriarchs produced the *Huiyan*; the third patriarch detailed the *Cui Zhuan*;
the fourth and fifth patriarchs recorded them in various commentaries. Upon examining and verifying these, there was not the slightest discrepancy.

Indeed, the Buddha transmitted the Dharma of the Mind to the successive patriarchs, and the patriarchs propagated this Dharma of the Mind throughout the Dharma-realm; thus, until the end of the future, the transformation of beings shall continue without interruption. Its...
Can the traces of the Way be without evidence? Without evidence, people will not believe; and if they do not believe, how can they emulate them?
Would this not be a cause for shame before the Buddhas and Patriarchs?

From this day forward, we know that the upholding and nurturing of the Buddha-dharma depends entirely upon the various Patriarchs, and the learning of the Patriarchal Way depends entirely upon the canonical records. Thus, this record is no small contribution.
He then ordered it to be carved so that it might be shared with all who appreciate it. May those who see or hear this and rejoice take care not to dismiss it as redundant talk.
Recorded by the Layman Fuchai of Hulin, Dai Jingzeng, for the *Brief Record of the Five Patriarchs of the Dharmadhātu School*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xufa of Ciyun Monastery in Qiantang.
The First Patriarch, Venerable Dushun:
His name was Fashun; his imperial title was Dixin. His secular surname was Du, and he was from Duling in Wannian County, Yongzhou.
He was a human being. He was born in the second year of Emperor Wu of Chen’s Yongding era. When he was only three days old, a wet nurse came of her own accord to nourish him.
When he reached the third month [of age], he ascended into the air and departed (1). During his childhood, he would frequently preach the Dharma upon a tomb behind his residence;
those who heard him could not fail to believe and attain awakening. Consequently, it was named the "Preaching Tomb" (2). At the age of fifteen, he took over...
His elder brother led troops to suppress the rebels. [The Master] provided ten thousand soldiers with more than enough water from buckets and firewood.
One night, he secretly took the soiled garments worn by those in the various camps and washed them all completely clean. Without raising a blade, the rebel raiders withdrew entirely.

Having no desire for official honor, he requested to return home to care for his parents (3). When he reached the age of eighteen, he went to the Yinseng Temple to serve under the Chan Master Wei Zhen.
He went to the master’s residence and requested ordination. The Chan Master personally shaved his head, at which time the earth shook;

the earth deities held out trays to receive his hair, and the fourfold assembly marveled at this (4). Later, while traveling to proselytize in Gyeongju, the host of a vegetarian feast invited only three hundred monks, yet suddenly five hundred poor people followed along to attend.
Fearing that the provisions would be insufficient, the host was concerned, but Shang said, "As long as the mind is impartial, it will suffice."
There was none who did not understand [the teaching]. When the fast was concluded, the five hundred people were transformed into arhats and departed on clouds (5).
Zhang Hongchang kept oxen and horses that were by nature extremely vicious; yet he showed them only kindness and compassion, so they no longer gored or bit (6).

When he led the assembly to Qijing on Mount Li to plant vegetables, there were many insects and ants in the ground; he then circled the boundaries to establish the demarcations, whereupon the insects...

He moved to the outskirts and was thus able to cultivate the land without harm (7). He still suffered from a swelling; when it burst and pus flowed out, someone who tasted it found its fragrance beyond compare.
Those who wiped it with silk cloth found the aroma did not dissipate. Soon he recovered, and he helped others eliminate their swellings (8).
A man from San Yuan County named Tian Sadāva had been deaf since birth; when called to him, he was immediately able to hear.
(9) Furthermore, Zhang Su also suffered from a congenital dumbness; upon being spoken to, he was immediately able to speak. (10) A monk in Wengong County was possessed by a venomous dragon.
When the community sought his aid, [the Master] sat facing him with hands folded in formal composure. The dragon then spoke through the afflicted monk, saying:

"Since the Chan Master has arrived, it is right that I do not remain for long. Shortly thereafter, the affliction was released. (11) Thus, the pestilences and miasmas of near and far, as well as the effects of lustful depravity, were [subdued].

As for those afflicted by vexations, there was none who did not seek him out; he would not employ any other methods, but simply directed them toward meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), and there were none whose ailments were not healed.
Even when it came to spirit trees and dragon temples, he would destroy them upon seeing them. As for the objects of worship for shamans and sorcerers, he personally eliminated them.
The people of the world all marveled at this and called him the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva" (12). From this, his reputation reached the imperial court during the Sui dynasty. Emperor Wen...

The Emperor accorded him profound faith and respect, providing him with a monthly stipend for his support (13). Later, while traveling to the South Mountain, he encountered the flooding of the River Heng.
His attendants were struck with fear, but Daoxuan led the multitude across together; the water then ceased its flow, and they passed over it by walking slowly.

As soon as they reached the bank, the water returned to its former state (14). At that time, during a ritual alms-round for a feast offering, the host of the ceremony was holding a child and requested that his calamities be dispelled and his life extended.
Shang looked at him intently and said, "This is your kinsman from a previous life; you must repent before him.

When the meal was finished, Shang ordered the child to be carried to the riverbank and threw him into the water. The husband and wife beat their breasts and wailed aloud, but Shang said, "Your son still lives."
He pointed at him with his finger, and the boy transformed into a man six feet tall who stood amidst the waves.
He rebuked him, saying, "In a previous life, you took my gold and silk and killed me by pushing me into the water.

Had it not been for the Bodhisattva who resolved our enmity, I would never have forgiven you. The husband and wife remained silent, filled with faith and submission. (15) By chance, he placed a pair of traveling shoes...
At the city gate, for three days, nothing was lost. When people asked him the reason, Shang said, "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have not stolen so much as a single coin from another;
such is the retribution. When those who had committed theft heard this, they all repented and changed their ways. (16)
He was by nature gentle and mild, and his conduct was lofty and pure. He had no fixed teacher and took the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary field of study.
Residing in seclusion at Mount Zhongnan, he subsequently composed the *Fajie Guan Wen* (Text on the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm) based on the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Once it was completed, he cast it into a great fire and prayed, saying: "If this accords with the holy mind, may not a single character be damaged. Suddenly, he felt the presence of the Bodhisattvas of the Ocean-like Assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*.
(17) "Sa. He manifested his body to offer praise; later, the fruit was not destroyed. At that time, among the disciples, only Zhiyan alone attained its profound mysteries.
There was a monk named Fan Xuanzhi, a native of Anding. In his youth, he practiced the Way in the capital. Later, he went south to serve as an eminent disciple.
[Zhiyan] still had him recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and exhorted him to practice the conduct of Samantabhadra according to the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā-mukha*. After a long time, every...

While reciting the sutras, śarīra relics were frequently obtained from his mouth; in total, there were several hundred grains (18). He once composed a verse on the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) which says:
"The ox in Jia Prefecture eats grass; the horse in Yi Prefecture has a bloated belly. Seeking a physician throughout the world, he applies moxibustion upon the left shoulder of a pig.
Even those who had thoroughly mastered the Chan of Bodhidharma would all roll back their tongues upon seeing this (19). Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty looked up to him with admiration.
The Emperor summoned Shen-de to enter the palace. Upon meeting him personally, the Emperor asked, "I have suffered from chills and fevers for a long time without recovery.
By what means can your divine power dispel them? Shang replied, "With Your Majesty’s virtue governing the realm, why worry over a minor ailment?

Simply issue a general amnesty, and Your Majesty’s person will naturally find peace. The Emperor followed this advice, and his illness was subsequently cured. Consequently, he was bestowed with the title "Imperial Heart" (Di-xin) within the palace.

20. [His] inner and outer ritual services were like those toward a Buddha. On the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, while presiding over the Yishan Temple at the southern suburb of Yongzhou for a universal assembly of those with karmic affinity, his countenance remained unchanged; suddenly, he spoke his farewell to the assembly. 21. [End.]

He entered the inner quarters once more to take leave of Emperor Taizong and ascended the Grand Terrace Hall, where he passed away upon the imperial couch. The Emperor kept him within the Great Palace for seven days of offerings;
at that time, his age was eighty-four. His remains appeared as if alive, and a wondrous fragrance occasionally issued forth. After one week had passed, [the body vanished].
An imperial edict was issued to have him escorted to the northern plains of Fanchuan, where a burial vault was excavated for his interment. This is the present-day Huisheng Monastery.
The capital city lamented together; mourning garments covered the fields. The color of his face within the shrine remained increasingly fresh even after a month had passed.
He sat peacefully for three weeks, his entire body remaining undispersed. A stupa was subsequently erected at Chang’an Nanhuayan Monastery (22). Even before he manifested final nirvana, one—
A disciple came to take his leave, saying, "I am going to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. Baoshang smiled and spoke this verse: "The traveler wanders aimlessly in waves;
At Mount Tai, he bows to an earthen slope. Mañjuśrī is just this very place— Where else would one seek Amitābha? The disciple did not understand and departed.
Only when he reached the foot of the mountain did he encounter an old man who asked, "Why have you come? He replied, "I have come to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. The old man said:
The Great Being had already departed for Chang’an to teach and transform sentient beings. [The monk] asked, “Who was this? He replied, “It was the Venerable Dushun.
The monk stood up straight and cried out in shock, “That was my teacher! In an instant, the old man vanished.

The monk hurried home, doubling his pace, but upon reaching the Shan River, it was swollen by a flood; he could not cross until three days later. When he arrived, the Master had already passed away the day before.
"Go! By this you may verify that he was an emanation-body of Mañjuśrī" (23). For further details, see the extensive biographies.
Regarding the Second Patriarch, Master Zhinan:
his dharma name was Zhinan; his secular surname was Zhao. He was born in the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era. His courtesy name was Yun... [text continues].

Master Hua resided in this temple, and thus it was named after him. He was also titled the Venerable Zhixiang (Supreme Reality), a name by which people continued to call him because he presided over its transformation.
He was exceptionally brilliant and outstanding, possessing a level of insight far beyond the ordinary. Upon seeing a scripture, he could recite it from memory without ever forgetting it.
When he first shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk, he made a vow before the Great Canon that he would draw out the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
First (Second). He then went to Mount Zhongnan to join the Venerable Dushun as his senior disciple. Before long after serving the Master, he fully grasped the essential principles.
The Venerable then transmitted to him the *Guānfǎ* (Methods of Contemplation) that he had compiled, instructing him to study it and teach it to others. (Third)

Later, as he desired to propagate [the teachings], he happened to encounter a strange monk who came and said to him, "If you wish to understand the Dharma-realm school (*dharmadhātu-naya*) of the One Vehicle of the *Avataṃsaka*, it is precisely the meaning of the 'six aspects' (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Be careful not to be negligent;

for one or two months, settle yourself in quietude and contemplate this, and you shall come to know it yourself. Having finished speaking, the monk suddenly vanished. Thereupon, he began his intensive study.
He studied them until, before even a month had passed, he attained sudden and complete penetration; he was twenty-seven years old at the time (5).

At Zhixiang Temple, he composed the five-fascicle *Huayan jing souxuan yi chao* (Annotated Commentary on the Profound Meaning Searched for in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), titled *Huayan jing zhong souxuan fenji tongzhi fanggui* (The Method for Penetrating Wisdom through the Classification of the Profound Meaning Searched for within the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
This work elucidates the six characteristics (*liu xiang*), opens up the ten mysteries (*shi xuan*), and establishes the five teachings (*wu jiao*) (6). At that time, in Jingzhao...
Huiyou of Chongfu Temple was rigorous and austere in his observance of the precepts. Admiring the Master’s virtue, he came specifically to attend upon him.

The Master instructed him to specialize in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Every dawn and at every auspicious night, he would burn incense and reverently recite the "Manifestation" chapter (*Prakṛtyabhisambodhi-parivarta*).
Later, he suddenly beheld more than ten bodhisattvas springing forth from the earth; their bodies were golden in color, all emitting radiance as they sat upon lotus flowers.

He sat down. With palms joined, he listened as this chapter was recited; when the sutra was finished, [the deity] vanished (7). In the fourth year of the Xianqing era, the Master lectured on the *Avataṃsaka* at Yunhua Temple.
His school’s influence flourished greatly, and his fame spread throughout the world. Monastics and laypeople, both clergy and laity, all paid him homage. At that time, Fazang was seventeen years old;
he had taken leave of his parents to seek the Dharma at Taibai Mountain. Later, hearing that his parents were ill, he departed.
Toku entered the capital. At midnight, he suddenly beheld a divine light that came to illuminate the courtyard and buildings.

He sighed, saying, "There must be extraordinary people who shall propagate the vast and great teaching. The following morning, after paying homage at the temple, he posed several questions; all of them were beyond the reach of ordinary thought.

The Master sighed in admiration and said, "Even among monks such as Yi Long and his peers, those who have yet to inquire into this principle are rare; how much more so for you, a virtuous and worthy man, to have opened up my ears and eyes!
Someone then informed him: "This is the layman Yunqi, who has long studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* while living on wild fruits; he has come to pay his respects to his compassionate parents."
Having just arrived here, I have savored the Venerable Master’s wondrous understanding and consider him my true teacher;

the Master, too, rejoices that the transmission of the torch has found its rightful recipient (8). In the second year of the Longshuo era, the Korean Master Uisang, together with Wonhyo, entered the land of the Great Tang.
While staying overnight at an ancient tomb, because Wonhyo had attained the principle of Mind-Only, he immediately returned to the new [teachings].
[The monk] Luo Xianggong came to Yunhua and paid homage to the Master, wishing to become his disciple and study together with Master Zang (9).

In the first year of the Zongzhang era, as the Master was about to pass away, Master Zang was still wearing lay clothing; the Master then entrusted Daocheng, Bocen, and other great virtuous ones, saying:
"This worthy one has set his mind upon the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. He has attained self-awakening without a teacher and shall continue to propagate my legacy."
As for the Dharma, it was solely due to this man that we were fortunate enough to receive his residual light and be granted access to the established regulations.
Later, he dreamed that the Prajñā Terrace had collapsed and the tall banner had also fallen. He told his disciples, "I shall now temporarily depart for the Pure Land.
Less than a month later, he preached the Dharma and passed away at the age of seventy-two. At that time, Yixiang transmitted the *Acintya-sūtra* and returned to the lands east of the sea.
Daehong was promoted by that country as the first patriarch of the *Avataṃsaka* school and was collectively titled Venerable Busi (11).
Later, during the Changshou era, Master Xuanzang sent a letter to Yixiang via Dharma Master Shengquan upon his return to Silla, stating:

"We shared the same causes in past lives and the same karma in this life, such that we have obtained this retribution and both have been bathed in the Great Scripture. We were especially favored by our former teacher, who bestowed this [upon us]."
This is an esoteric manual. May those who encounter this work use it to form causes for future lives.

However, because the *Heshang* commentary is rich in meaning yet concise in expression, it has made it difficult for later generations to enter its depths. Therefore, I have recorded these subtle words and wondrous principles in their entirety, compiling them into this *Yiji* (Record of Meaning).

I transmit this to that land; I hope you will graciously grant me your admonitions and instructions. I imagine you have been sequestered in your room for contemplation, and only after ten days have passed do you emerge.
You summoned your disciples Zhen-ding, Xiang, Yuan-liang, and Shi-biao—four men in all—and had them each lecture on the *Tanxuan ji* (Record of Exploring the Profound), ten fascicles each.
He addressed them, saying: "Master Cang has broadened my understanding; it is you who inspire me. Each of you should exert yourselves; do not [be complacent]."
It was indeed a deception. Consequently, the teachings were transmitted throughout the nation and learning spread across the ten mountains;
all of this was due to the power of Master Yunhua’s Dharma transformation (12). His divine wonders and virtuous conduct are fully recorded in the *Ganying zhuan* (Accounts of Miraculous Responses).
The Third Patriarch, National Teacher Xianshou:
His posthumous name was Fazang and his courtesy name was Xianshou. The Emperor bestowed upon him the honorary title "National One Dharma Master" (Guoyi Fashi). His secular surname was Kang.
His ancestors were people of the former kingdom of Kangju, serving as ministers of that state in successive generations of high office.

His grandfather came from Kangju to pay court, divining the favorable winds of our sagely era. His father’s name was Mi; the Taizong Emperor posthumously conferred upon him the title of Left Attendant-in-Ordinary.

His younger brother’s name was Baozang, who served as Court Counselor during the reign of the Zhongzong Emperor and acted as the Supervisor of Tongwan. When the Master was conceived, his mother dreamed of swallowing the sun’s radiance before becoming pregnant.
He was born on the second day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era (2). Upon his birth, he aspired to the unsurpassed [enlightenment].

When he reached the age of sixteen in the third year of the Xianqing era, he offered a finger by performing a ritual offering before the Śarīra stupa at Famen Temple in Qizhou, vowing to awaken to the Buddha Vehicle (3).
The following year, his resolve sharpened, he sought out a teacher and subsequently took his leave.
His father sought the Dharma at Mount Taibai, where he studied various Vaipulya scriptures. Later, hearing that his compassionate parents were displeased, he returned to serve them at home.
As the years passed, he was able to exhaust all his efforts in this service. At that time, Venerable Yan was lecturing on the Mahāyāna sūtras at Yunhua;
the Master paid him homage as a disciple and delved deeply into the inexhaustible teachings. This occurred in the first year of the Zongzhang era, when the Master was twenty-six years old.
He went to the Venerable Śikṣānanda to request and receive the Bodhisattva precepts. The assembly told him, "This layman can recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and also lecture on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.

The Venerable one marveled and said, "If merely upholding the single chapter on 'Pure Conduct' (*Śīlaparivarta*) has already allowed one to obtain the great Bodhisattva precepts, how much more so for one who possesses such an understanding of its meaning?
(6) In the first year of the Xianheng era, when the Master was twenty-eight years old, it happened that...
Lady Yang of the Rongguo family passed away. Empress Wu extensively cultivated fields of merit and donated her residence to establish Taoyuan Monastery.
The various great virtuous ones (mahāsattvas) residing there submitted a joint petition to recommend Master Yan, who had been entrusted with the late master’s legacy.
Consequently, by imperial decree, he was ordained at the Taoyuan Dharma Hall and subsequently appointed as its abbot. In the first year of the Shangyuan era, an edict was issued ordering—

The ten virtuous masters (*da-de*) of the capital city conferred the full precepts upon the Master and bestowed upon him the title "Xianshou" (this being the practice of using a pen-name as a formal title).

Furthermore, the Emperor issued an edict for the Master to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* at Taiyuan Temple. On the Dragon Boat Festival, Empress Wu dispatched an envoy to present him with five sets of monastic robes.
In the fifth month of the first year of the Tiàolù era, Hé Róngshī of Wànnián County in Yōngzhōu died suddenly after consuming an incalculable number of chicken eggs.

Together with seven hundred others, he entered the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons. A messenger from the underworld returned to life to instruct his fourth son, Xíngzhèng, to earnestly petition the Master to redeem their sins.
The Master ordered that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* be recited and transcribed. This continued until the eighth month of the first year of the Yǒnglóng era.
In the [first] month, he completed the transcription of the *Zhuāngyán* (The Adornment). He invited monks for a vegetarian feast and repentance ceremony;

there, the assembled congregation saw the master Hé Róng and seven hundred ghostly followers arrive at the banquet hall to pay their respects (9). Regarding the translations from the Jin dynasty, the Master had always lamented that they were incomplete and deficient.

That year, Tripiṭaka Master Rìzhào arrived in the capital bringing Sanskrit manuscripts. Emperor Gāozōng issued an edict for him to translate the sūtras and śāstras at the West Temple of the Wèiguó Monastery. The Master...
He went to visit him and inquire. Huizhao said, "The eighth assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* has also arrived here.

He then compared it with the Tripiṭaka master’s version and indeed obtained the passages concerning the ten virtuous friends, such as Sudhana seeking the Light of the Lord of Heaven (*Devendraprabha*). He subsequently requested a translation to supplement the missing portions.
At the West Taiyuan Temple, he translated two missing sections from within the "Dharmadhātu Chapter": the first was from [the section on] Lady Māyā...
Behind the person [i.e., Sudhana] and before Maitreya Bodhisattva, in between, are the ten spiritual friends beginning with Devendraprabha.

Second, from behind Maitreya Bodhisattva, extending to the presence of as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, in between, Mañjuśrī extends his hand across one hundred and ten *yojanas* to touch the crown of Sudhana’s head. This is according to these sixty fascicles.

10. Regarding the translation of the *Samādhi-sūtra*: Recently, having received the imperial decree, I, together with the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman, the Vinaya Master Daocheng, the Dharma Master Bochen, the Dharma Master Mahāyānabhadra, and others, translated more than ten works, including the *Guhyavibhūṣaṇa-sūtra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, totaling twenty-four fascicles.
The Dharma Master Falin polished the prose, and the Dharma Master Huizhi transcribed the oral translation. 11. Regarding the translation of the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*.
In the fourth month of the first year of the Yongchun era, a man named Guo Shenliang from Chang’an County in Yongzhou was practicing the pure conduct when he died suddenly.
The devas led him to the Inner Court of Tuṣita, where he paid homage to Maitreya. A bodhisattva there said to him, "Why do you not uphold the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*?
Shenliang declined on the grounds that there was no one to explain it, to which the bodhisattva replied, "There is currently the Bodhisattva Xianshou [Fazang]."

To propagate [the Dharma]. How could one say it does not exist? (12) In the first year of the Wénmíng era, while the Master was at the West Taiyuán Monastery with the Tripiṭaka Master Sūryavarman during a break from translating scriptures, he personally asked:
"Did the ancient masters of the Western Regions distinguish between the provisional and the ultimate within the holy teachings of a single lifetime?
He replied: "In recent times, there were two masters of śāstras in India: one was named Śīlabhadra, who inherited the lineage of Maitreya."

Asanga, who was a contemporary of Dharmapāla and Nanda, established the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiangzong). Two others, both named Jñānaprabha, were distant successors of Mañjuśrī and Nāgārjuna, and proximate disciples of Qingmu (Vimalamitra) and Bhāviveka;
they established the Dharma-svabhāva school (Faxingzong). From this point on, the doubts regarding the classification of the teachings were resolved (13).
At that time, the two virtuous masters Cheng and Chen asked: "There was a man named Wang Minggan in Jingzhao who died and entered hell; what did Dizang Bodhisattva teach him?"
He recited a verse, saying: "If one wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate in this way:

the mind creates all Tathāgatas. Upon entering the audience with King Yama, the King heard this and released him. He regained consciousness only after three days and recounted the matter to Master Ding of Kōngguān Monastery.
However, he did not know whether there was a way to escape. The Master replied, "This is from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra."
The fourth is the verse from the *Yāma-sabhā* section; upon examination, it is indeed a set of ten stanzas (14).
In the second year of the Chuigong era, the Master lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Cien Monastery (15).

On the fourth day of the second month of the first year of the Yongchang era, he encountered the Khotanese Tripiṭaka Master Indravarman at Dongsi in Weiguo, the Divine Capital, who informed him that the śrāmaṇera Prajñā...

(16) Míjiábo ascended to heaven and recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, whereby he was able to break the ranks of the asuras. (17) In the first year of Tiānshòu, he went to visit his relatives in Xiàzhōu;

neither the prefectural governor nor the district magistrates failed to welcome him from the outskirts of the city. (18) In the second year of Tiānshòu, the prefect and magistrates of Zēngzhōu welcomed him to lecture on the Great Scripture (*Mahāvaipulya*).
During the discussion between the heterodox and the orthodox, there was a follower of left-handed paths in the assembly who did not believe in the Buddha-dharma. His mouth—

He uttered evil words, and suddenly blisters broke out on his body and face; his eyebrows and beard were completely rotted away. He came in haste to seek repentance. The Master admonished and exhorted him, saying:
"This is merely the 'flower retribution' [the initial sign]. You must pay homage to the Triple Gem and reverently recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* one hundred times; then your sin may be extinguished."
Before he had finished half of his recitation of the sutra, his physical form remained as it was before (18).

During the Changshou era, while the Master was lecturing on the *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* at Yunhua Monastery, a radiance emerged from his mouth and in an instant formed into a canopy, as recorded by the multitude (19).

In the first year of the Yanchai era, when he reached the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*), celestial flowers scattered in all directions and five-colored clouds coalesced in the sky, continuing without ceasing throughout the morning, their fragrance and colors [filling the air].

As the Master ascended the seat, he declared: "How great is the True Realm! It is the source from which the myriad dharmas arise; it encompasses both emptiness and existence."

Yet it transcends all marks; entering the realm of words and images, it leaves no trace. Our Buddha attained this, wondrously practicing true awakening and utterly eradicating the habits of defilement.
He merged his body with the world-systems so they mutually contain one another, and his voice and light radiate afar to illuminate all. Our Emperor has attained this as well:

his spiritual discernment reaches the ultimate void, he preserves and harmonizes the Great Harmony, his sacred writings eclipse those of a hundred kings, and his pure influence fans out across the myriad nations. *The Avataṃsaka Sūtra*...
Thus, one exhausts this essential purpose and completes its source and flow; therefore, it is vast and expansive, profound and deep, beyond the reach of thought or deliberation.
To lose its essential purpose is to labor in vain through kalpas of eons; to find its gateway is to attain the truth.

To equalize all Buddhas in a single morning, one must contemplate a single speck of dust; then the entire Dharma-realm rests in the palm of one’s hand. The principle is profound and wisdom far-reaching, yet my consciousness is dim and my words meager.

Having defiled Your Majesty’s sagely intelligence, I shall now withdraw from my seat. At that time, the Emperor remained in silent, ocean-like stillness, attaining a vast and luminous great awakening.

He turned to his ministers and said: "The teachings of my Master are elegant yet concise, and his expressions are classical yet profound. He fans the true wind within the realm of the First Noble Truth;
he is able to cool my heart with the Holy Dharma. I shall therefore bestow upon him the title 'Master of the Nation' (Guoshi), using 'Cooling' (Qingliang) as part of it.
(24) Consequently, the high officials and ministers of both the inner and outer courts all honored him as their teacher with the rites of the Eight Precepts.

(25) At that time, Emperor Shunzong was in the Eastern Palace. He sent a letter regarding the essentials of the mind, treating [the recipient] as his teacher. The Master replied in a letter, saying: "The Ultimate Way is rooted in the One Mind;
the Dharma of the mind is rooted in non-abiding. The essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous awareness that is never obscured.

Its nature and characteristics are quiescent, encompassing all virtues and functions. When one is deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), afflictions and suffering arise in confusion; when one awakens to the true nature, it is empty."
It is luminous, vast, and penetrating; though it is "the mind itself is the Buddha," only those who have realized it know this.

Furthermore, he requested that [Zongmi] compose one fascicle on the *Nītārtha* (Definitive Meaning) and an essay on the causes and conditions for the transgression of eating meat (26). In the first year of the Yongzhen era, Shunzong ascended the imperial throne.

The Emperor issued an edict for the Master at Xingtang Temple to construct the Puguang Hall, the Huayan Pavilion, and the sculpted Womb-World (Huazang) stupa, and to depict the Assembly of the Dharma-realm (27).
In the second year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong, the Prince of Nankang, Wei Xie, and the Chancellor Wu Yuanheng [commissioned these works].
*Qingzhuo Fajieguan Xuanjing* (One Scroll), Number Twenty-Eight. In the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, an imperial edict summoned the Master to the inner palace to discourse on the Dharma.

The Emperor asked: "Regarding that which is elucidated by the *Avataṃsaka*, what is meant by the 'Dharmadhātu'? The Master replied: "The Dharmadhātu is the fundamental essence of the body and mind of all sentient beings.
From the very beginning, it has been numinous, luminous, vast, and profoundly tranquil; it is solely one."
It is simply the true realm. It has no form or appearance, yet it pervades the great trichiliocosm; it has no boundaries, yet it encompasses all phenomena.
It is vividly manifest within the heart and mind, yet its form cannot be seen; it shines brilliantly amidst the sensory objects of form, yet its principle cannot be divided.
Without the eye of wisdom that penetrates all phenomena and the clear intelligence free from conceptual thought, one cannot perceive it.
One's own mind is thus so spiritually penetrating. Therefore, when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed: "How marvelous!
I now see that all sentient beings universally possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it.
Thereupon, in accordance with the nature of the Dharma-realm, he preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which is entirely based on true emptiness.

Discerning the emotional mind, phenomena and principle are harmoniously integrated; pervasive and profoundly tranquil—this is called the Great Principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Having heard this profound discourse, Emperor Wuzong attained a vast realization within himself.

He immediately issued an edict to the relevant authorities to cast a special golden seal and conferred upon him the title of *Sengtong* (Patriarch of the Monks) and *Qingliang Guoshi* (National Teacher Qingliang).
He was appointed to preside over all monastics under heaven and to oversee the affairs of the Buddhist Gate. (29) [The reigns of] Emperor Muzong and Emperor Jingzong followed.
All looked up to his immense virtue. He was posthumously bestowed the title State Preceptor Dazhao (30).

In the fifth year of the Tahe era of Emperor Wenzong, the Emperor received the mind-precepts from the Master and vowed never to eat clams (31). In the first year of the Kaicheng era, the Emperor celebrated the Master’s hundredth birthday.

He was granted robes, wealth, food, and delicacies, and was conferred the title of Grand State Preceptor (32). He lectured on the Great Sūtras fifty times, both before and after [his ordination] (33).
He established fifteen Unrestricted Great Assemblies (34). As for his writings that have been transmitted to the present day:
In total, there are over four hundred fascicles. Prime Minister Qi Kang, Zheng Yuying, and Gao Ying requested that he compose the *Huayan Gangyao* (Essentials of the Avataṃsaka) in three fascicles.
Prime Minister Li Jifu, Court Gentleman for Ceremonial Affairs Gui Deng, and Prince Consort Du Cong requested that he write the *Zhengyao* (Essential Points) in one fascicle.
Grand Marshal Gao Chongwen requested that he author the *Jingdeng Shuowen* (Explanations of the Mirror-Lamp) in one fascicle. Minister of Education Yan Rou and Minister of Works... [text continues]
Zheng Yuan; the Provincial Inspector Lu Changyuan, who requested the composition of one scroll titled *The Contemplation on the Perfect Interfusion of the Three Sages*;
the Military Governor Xue Hua; the Surveillance Commissioner Meng Jian; Qian Hui of the Secretariat; the Reminder Bai Juyi; and the Palace Secretary Du Gao, among others.
He requested the compilation of the *Ten-Scroll Exposition on the Heart-Mirror Diagram of the Flower Treasury Realm of the Seven Locations and Nine Assemblies*.

Furthermore, together with the Master Ling Sui, Director of the Sangha, eighteen head seat-holders, and eminent practitioners of the Three Studies from ten monasteries, he compiled more than thirty works on the essential lineages of the *Avataṃsaka*, *Complete Enlightenment*, *Four Divisions of the Vinaya*, and *Madhyamaka* scriptures and treatises.
He also composed the *Exhaustive Exposition of the Definitive Meaning of the Great Sūtra*.

Essentials in three fascicles; Discourses on the Sūtras and Treatises delivered before the Emperor on the Anniversary of the Seven Sages’ Birth, together with his own family’s poems, letters, and memorials, totaling more than eighty fascicles (thirty-five).
Among his disciples who became teachers themselves, there were thirty-eight, headed by Haidaian Jiguang.
His students who received his instruction numbered one thousand, including specifically Sengrui of the Eastern Capital and Zongmi of Mount Gui.
He alone attained its profound mysteries; all others came with empty hearts and departed with full bellies (36).

On the sixth day of the third month in the third year of the Kaicheng era, he summoned his senior disciples, including the Chief Seat of the Three Teachings, the Great Master Baoyin Hai'an, and others, and instructed them, saying:

I have heard that when fortune is merely coincidental, it brings no merit; the former sages lamented this. When one returns to simplicity without virtuous conduct, the ancients felt shame for such a person.

Without the distinction of ancestral order (zhāomù) in movement and stillness, and without the continuity of the threads of tradition in their coming and going, do not engage in the excavation of heterodox views; do not follow what is wrong or argue over the false;

do not allow yourself to be deluded and ensnared by an evil mind; and do not stubbornly persist in contention. Even the Great Illumination cannot dispel the darkness of a long night, nor can a compassionate mother...
"To ensure the safety of your descendants after you have passed away, you should place your trust in the Buddha and not place your trust in men. The True Realm is profound and subtle;
it is not manifested through words and speech, but must be realized through deep resolve so that it appears clearly before one.

If, when facing objects, you remain without a [discursive] mind, and when encountering conditions, you remain unmoved, then you will not have failed me. Having finished speaking, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away. (37) The Master’s life spanned nine...

In the morning, he served as the Preceptor to seven emperors. His secular age was one hundred and two; his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-lakṣa*) was eighty-three. His discourse was elegant and refined; his deportment served as a model for others.

His learning encompassed the nine schools of thought, and his talent could supply two pens at once. He observed the practice of eating only once throughout his life and did not store away any surplus (38).
Emperor Wenzong, out of profound reverence for this ancestral sage, specifically suspended court for three days, and his high ministers wore white mourning garments (39). [He] shed [his mortal coil].

After twenty-one days, his countenance became increasingly radiant. He sat upright with a majesty as imposing as a mountain. On the twenty-seventh day of that month, by imperial decree, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan.

During the initial period [of mourning], a foreign monk arrived at the capital and submitted a memorial stating that he had seen two messengers on the Pamir Mountains passing through the air; he had stopped them with a mantra and questioned them, and they replied: "We are..."
He was a deity of the Mañjuśrī Hall in North India. From the Eastern Land (China), he took a great tooth of the Avataṃsaka Bodhisattva and returned to his country to offer it.
An imperial decree was issued to open the stūpa and verify this; indeed, one tooth had vanished, and only thirty-nine remained.
They were as brilliant as frost, their features appearing as if alive. He was subsequently cremated, and several thousand śarīra relics were obtained, which were luminous, clear, and lustrous.

(43) His tongue was like a red lotus; fire could not alter it. (44) The Emperor issued an edict for his posthumous title, styling him the National Teacher Qingliang (also known as the National Teacher by this title).
(45) He was granted the inscription "Myōkaku" (Wondrous Enlightenment) for his stupa. (46) An imperial decree ordered the Chancellor Pei Xiu to compose the commemorative stele inscription.
(47) An imperial edict commanded the painting of the National Teacher’s portrait, which was enshrined at Daxingtang Temple. Emperor Wenzong personally composed a eulogy for the image.
Eulogy in Eight Chapters (48). The remainder is as found in other biographies.
Regarding the Fifth Patriarch, Master Guifeng:
his posthumous name was Zongmi, and his style name was Guifeng. Because the Master resided on this mountain, he acquired this title. During the Jianzhong era of Emperor Dezong...
He was born in the first year of the [Yuanhe] era. He was a native of Xichong County in Guozhou. His secular surname was He. For generations, his family had followed the Confucian profession (1).

When the Master was still a young child, he mastered Confucian learning; by the time he reached his early adulthood, he studied the sutras and śāstras, abstained from meat and pungent vegetables, and associated closely with virtuous Chan masters (2).
In the second year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong, while he was about to go to the capital for the imperial examinations, he happened to encounter Daoyuan of Dayun Temple in Suizhou.
At the Dharma seat of a Zen master, he asked about the Dharma and found his mind in accord with it, like a needle meeting its eye-pin. He then requested to shave his head and don the robes;
at that time, he was twenty-seven years old (3). While serving as a śrāmaṇera, one day he followed the assembly of monks to a meal at the home of Ren Guan, a local official.

The Master sat in the lowest seat and received the transmission of the scriptures in due order. Upon obtaining the twelve chapters of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), he read one or two chapters and attained a sudden, great awakening.
His body and mind leaped with joy, and he returned to report this to Yuán. Yuán said, "These scriptures were bestowed upon you by all the Buddhas.
You shall greatly propagate the teaching of Perfect and Sudden [Enlightenment]. Go now; do not remain stagnant in a single corner. Thereupon, in that same year, he received full ordination.
Jie took his leave upon receiving these instructions and went to visit Chan Master Zhong of Jingnan. Zhong said, "You are a person who transmits the teachings.

He then visited Chan Master Zhao of Luoyang. Zhao said, "You are a person among the Bodhisattvas" (5). In the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, he arrived at Xianghan and met the Acharya Lingfeng of Huikuo Temple, who was ill;
from him, he received the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* composed by National Teacher Qingliang.
There were twenty fascicles of the *Śāstra* and forty fascicles of the *Great Commentary*. Upon reading them, he said with joy: "In my Chan practice I have encountered the Southern School;
in the teachings I have met the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*. Under a single word, the ground of my mind has opened up; within a single scroll, the sky of its meaning shines brightly.
Now that I have further obtained this Great Dharma, how fortunate I am! He then lectured on them for the assembly once (6). This was in the sixth year of the Yuanhe era.
He traveled to the Eastern Capital to pay homage at the ancestral pagodas and took up residence at Yongmu Temple. At the repeated request of the fourfold assembly, he lectured for a second time.
Among the disciples was one named Taigong, who, overcome with the joy of such a rare encounter, severed his own arm as an offering of gratitude.

Because the Master had not yet visited Qingliang Mountain, he composed a letter in one scroll, along with an essay titled "An Account of the Key Points and Vital Lineages within the Newly Compiled Commentaries and Sub-commentaries."
From afar, he recounted the rites of his disciples and dispatched his attendants Xuanguī and Zhìhuī to hasten with the petition to the Master. The Master immediately issued a reply, stating:

"To receive the ultimate meaning without meeting in person and without oral transmission, yet for its intent to be bound within this written expression as if it were my own heart—this has never occurred before.

This is not achieved by relying on sacred power alone, but must surely depend upon past causes. One may take the true son of a Wheel-Turning King as a metaphor; if I were to meet you face-to-face, I would seal [your realization]."
"His bonds were already severed; what more could be added? (8) When the lectures concluded, he went to the capital to pay his respects to the National Preceptor Qingliang.
The Preceptor said, "As for the Vairocana Flower Treasury [Pure Land], who else but you could follow me in its exploration? For the first two years, he attended upon him day and night.
Thereafter, although he engaged in doctrinal discussions at various monasteries, whenever he had doubts, he would go back and forth to consult and resolve them without ceasing. (9)

After several years of requesting further instruction, in the spring of the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era, while at Zhijusi Temple on Mount Zhongnan, he produced the *Yuanjue kewen* (Outline of the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra) and the *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium) in two fascicles. He vowed not to descend from the mountain and spent three years reading the entire Tripitaka.

His vows were fulfilled. In the fourteenth year, at Kōfuku-ji Temple, he produced one fascicle of the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra-kārikā-vyākhyā* (Jingang zuanyao shu) and one fascicle of its commentary (*chao*).
In the spring of the fifteenth year, at the two temples of Xingfu and Baoshou in the Capital, he compiled two fascicles of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Weishi shu).
(13) In the first year of the Changqing era, he retired to live at Caotang Monastery in Huxian. (14) In the spring of the second year, he re-edited his commentary on the *Niyuanjue jing*.
Furthermore, at Fengde Monastery on the Southern Mountains, he composed the *Huayan lun guan* in five fascicles. (15) In the summer of the third year.

At Fengde Temple, he compiled the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* in three fascicles (16). By the beginning of winter, his work on the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* was completed, consisting of the *Great Commentary* in three fascicles and the *Great Abstract* in thirteen fascicles (17).
Subsequently, he also annotated the *Abridged Commentary* in two fascicles and the *Small Abstract* in six fascicles.

He further composed the *Ritual for Cultivation and Realization at the Dharma Hall* in eighteen fascicles (18). On the National Birthday of the second year of the Taihe era, the Emperor... [text ends].
The Emperor summoned him to the inner palace and inquired about the essentials of all dharmas. He was granted a purple robe and bestowed with the imperial title of "Dade" (19).
Court officials, scholars, and commoners alike all looked up to him in reverence; only the Chancellor Pei Xiu had penetrated deeply into the inner sanctum to serve as his patron (20).
When the Minister of Revenue Wen Zao of Shan-nan asked, "For one who has awakened to principle and stilled delusion, karma is no longer bound. When such a person’s single lifetime comes to an end—"
After this, upon what does the spiritual nature rely? The Master said: "All sentient beings are without exception possessed of the awakened nature.

Its luminous clarity and empty stillness are no different from that of the Buddha. However, because since beginningless kalpas they have never attained realization, they falsely cling to the body as the mark of self.
Thus, they give rise to emotions such as attachment and aversion; following these emotions they create karma, and following their karma they receive retribution—birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Though one wanders through saṃsāra for long kalpas, the awakened nature within the body has never undergone birth or death.
It is like being driven and enslaved in a dream, while the body remains fundamentally at ease; or like water in a pond turning to ice, while its moist nature remains unchanged.

If one can awaken to this nature, it is the Dharmakāya, which is inherently unborn—how could there be any dependence? Although the absolute truth may be suddenly realized, deluded emotions are difficult to eradicate.

Eliminate them completely. One must maintain constant vigilance. Diminish them further and still further; one may take only emptiness and stillness as one's own essence. Do not identify with the physical body.
Take spiritual awareness as one's own mind; do not identify with deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all.

At the moment of death, karma itself can no longer bind them; although they possess an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), their destination is free and unfettered, allowing them to take up residence at will among gods or humans.
Once the thoughts of attachment and aversion have been extinguished, they no longer receive a body subject to the cycle of birth and death (*pratisaṃdhi*).

If the subtle flow of mentation is stilled, then the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) shines forth clearly, manifesting transformations according to the capacities of beings;

this is called "Buddha. The verse says: To perform deeds that accord with what is meaningful is the awakened mind; to perform deeds that accord with what is meaningless is the deluded and chaotic mind.
Madness follows the whims of one's thoughts; at the moment of death, one is dragged away by karma. Awakening does not arise from emotion; at the moment of death, one can transform karma (21).

Before and after, he was devoted to the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith), the *Lanpen jing* (Ullambana Sūtra), the *Xingyuan wang* (King of Vows), the *Fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm), and other sūtras, śāstras, commentaries, and sub-commentaries.

Furthermore, he compiled the sayings on Chan from various schools into the *Chanyuan zhuquanji duxu* (General Preface to the Collection of Passages on the Source of Chan), as well as letters, verses, and treatises in response to inquiries. In total—

(22) In more than ninety fascicles, on the sixth day of the first month of the first year of the Huichang era of Emperor Wuzong, he instructed his disciples at Xingfu Monastery to carry his corpse away to be given to birds and beasts, and to cremate his bones and scatter them. Having finished speaking, he sat and passed away.
(23) On the twenty-second day of that month, the clergy and laity enshrined his whole body at Guifeng and performed a cremation, from which śarīra were obtained.
There were several dozen grains, all white and lustrous. After the fire had subsided, his disciples wept as they sought them out, finding them all within the ashes and embers;
he then enshrined them in a stone chamber. He lived for sixty-two years in this world and maintained thirty-four years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-varṣa*).
Among his disciples—the fourfold assembly of monks and nuns—those who attained liberation numbered several thousand. The Chancellor Pei Xiu composed the inscription for his memorial stele.

In brief: "The single mind" is the totality of all phenomena (*dharmas*). When divided, it becomes concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); when expanded, it becomes the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); and when dispersed, it becomes the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*).
The myriad practices have never been anything other than the single mind, and the single mind has never contravened the myriad practices.

Therefore, for the Chan Master’s practice of the Way, he takes insight and vision as his gateway to the Dharma (*dharmamukha*), and takes tranquil stillness as its true flavor. Compassion and patience—

Wisdom serves as armor; the sword and spear of discernment subdue the heterodox and the impure, and untie the bonds of entanglement. That the impoverished son does not return and the destitute woman does not become wealthy—this brings shame upon our Teacher.
That the Three Vehicles do not flourish and the Four Divisions of the Sangha do not prosper—this brings shame upon our Teacher.

Loyalty and filial piety cannot be cultivated simultaneously; the burden of both is too heavy for one to bear. My Master felt ashamed of this, and thus he was earnestly intent on rescuing others and zealously engaged in guiding and enlightening them.
He did not exalt himself because of a single practice, nor did he tower above others because of a single virtue.

When someone sought refuge with him, he would go to meet them without waiting for an invitation. When someone sought to increase their understanding, he would open his teaching to them before they even reached a state of frustration. This was true even for children.
In his youth, he was not fastidious in his social interactions; though haughty and stubborn, he never grew weary of being exhorted and encouraged.

He was truly a bodhisattva entrusted by the Tathāgata and a virtuous friend to sentient beings who did not even ask for one. Is he not one of the four reliances? Is he not a person of the ten stages (daśabhūmi)?
(25) During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he was posthumously honored with the title Chan Master Anhui, and his stupa was named "Blue Lotus" (Qinglian). This is recorded in detail. (26)
